html:
The battle of the Hydaspes was fought in 326 BCE on the Hydaspes river, today's Jhelum in Pakistani Punjab, between Alexander the Great and the Indian king Porus. It was the last great battle of Alexander's conquests.

Porus held the far bank with an army that included war elephants. During the monsoon rains, Alexander made feints for days, then crossed the swollen river by night some way upstream. In the battle his cavalry broke the Indian flanks, and his infantry fought the elephants with long pikes. The elephants, wounded and panicking, trampled both sides.

Porus fought on until he was badly wounded. According to the Greek writers, when asked how he wished to be treated, he answered "like a king". Alexander kept him as ruler and gave him more land.

Soon after, at the Hyphasis river, Alexander's tired army refused to go further east, and he turned back. The Greek garrisons he left did not last; within a few years Chandragupta Maurya took the Punjab into his new empire, as the region had earlier passed under Persian rule.
